It permits municipalities to voluntarily submit the same data, requires counties to make reports publicly available, and directs the Maryland Department of Planning to publish the data on an interactive, searchable website and submit annual reports to the Governor and General Assembly.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Planning
qa_results.stakeholders: Counties with at least 150,000 residents, local planning and zoning departments, municipalities, residential housing developers, and the general public.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $86,109 in FY 2026 for the Maryland Department of Planning to hire one GIS administrator to build and maintain the permit database and online dashboard, increasing to $116,500 by FY 2030. State revenues are unaffected. Local government expenditures for reporting counties and voluntary municipalities are expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Planning is the primary implementing agency for the bill, tasked with collecting quarterly housing development permit reports from local jurisdictions, maintaining an interactive and searchable public website to display the data, reporting annually to the Governor and General Assembly, and adopting implementing regulations. It also incurs general fund expenditures to hire staff for these duties.

The Department of Housing and Community Development is a co-recipient of annual residential building permit application reports under existing provisions of the amended statute, and the bill directly affects statewide housing supply and development data relevant to its core mission.
The Department of Planning is mandated to submit an annual report on the building permit data collected under the bill to the Governor.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters the governance, planning, and reporting requirements of the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission (WSSC). The bill designates the Director of the Montgomery County Department of Environmental Protection (or designee) as an uncompensated, voting commissioner; requires WSSC to submit long-range financial plans with economic stress testing; mandates independent budget approval and triennial peer reviews for the WSSC Office of the Inspector General; requires independent evaluations of WSSC's efficiency and sustainability; and expands public reporting regarding customer billing disputes, high bill adjustments, and bond ratings.
qa_results.responsible_party: Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission (WSSC)
qa_results.stakeholders: WSSC customers and ratepayers in Montgomery and Prince George's counties, WSSC leadership and staff, the WSSC Office of the Inspector General, and county officials in Montgomery and Prince George's counties.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill does not materially affect State operations or finances. WSSC can implement the bill's requirements using existing resources, and WSSC revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires an independent evaluation of the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission (WSSC) that specifically reviews the regulatory oversight role played by the Public Service Commission regarding WSSC rates, charges, and assessments under § 25-105 of the Public Utilities Article.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill authorizes the governing body of a county, municipal corporation, or Baltimore City to expand an existing local-option property tax credit for disabled or fallen public safety officers, their surviving spouses, or cohabitants to include disabled or fallen judicial officers and correctional officers.
qa_results.responsible_party: Governing bodies of counties and municipal corporations, and the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City
qa_results.stakeholders: Disabled judicial officers, correctional officers, surviving spouses and cohabitants of fallen judicial and public safety officers, and local governments throughout Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Local property tax revenues may decrease beginning in FY 2026 to the extent that local jurisdictions elect to provide the credit and additional individuals qualify. The exact fiscal impact cannot be reliably estimated, though approximately 700 judicial officers and over 4,750 correctional officers work in Maryland. Local expenditures are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill expands local property tax credit eligibility to judicial officers who become permanently disabled or are killed in active service or in the course of employment, as well as their surviving spouses and cohabitants. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides administrative, operational, and personnel support for the state judicial branch.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill clarifies and incorporates correctional officers into the definition of public safety officers eligible for the disabled or fallen property tax credit. DPSCS employs state correctional officers who may qualify under local provisions enacted pursuant to this law.

qa_results.bill_summary: Known as Ace's Law, the bill requires public schools, nonpublic schools, the Maryland School for the Blind, and the Maryland School for the Deaf to notify a parent or guardian on the same day if a student attempts or accomplishes an elopement from the school campus. It also requires schools or a student's Individualized Education Program (IEP) team to review and address wandering or elopement behavior at least annually when updating a student's IEP or behavior intervention plan.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education and local school systems
qa_results.stakeholders: Public and nonpublic school students (especially those with IEPs or behavioral intervention plans), parents and guardians, school administrators, teachers, and IEP teams.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State operations or finances. The impact on local school systems is minimal, with minor additional staff time required for compliance beginning in FY 2026.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly defines the Maryland School for the Deaf as one of the covered schools subject to the statutory requirements to provide same-day notification to parents or guardians upon student elopement and to review and address wandering or elopement behaviors in IEPs or behavior intervention plans.

The Maryland State Department of Education oversees public elementary, middle, and high schools across the state as well as nonpublic special education placements and statewide IEP and behavior intervention plan standards, which are directly governed by the requirements of this bill.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill alters the compensation structure for the student member of the Montgomery County Board of Education by providing compensation divided between a higher education scholarship and a stipend based on percentages of an elected member's annual compensation. It also specifies that any future salary increases for elected members must take effect at the start of a term and cannot increase during the term.
qa_results.responsible_party: Montgomery County Board of Education
qa_results.stakeholders: The student member and elected members of the Montgomery County Board of Education, as well as Montgomery County Public Schools.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State Effect: None. Local Effect: The bill has no material effect on Montgomery County Board of Education expenditures, as it does not alter total compensation amounts, only the timing, structure, and form of compensation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Education Article regarding the compensation and stipend/scholarship options for the student member of the Montgomery County Board of Education. While MSDE oversees the state's public education system and local school boards, this measure is strictly local to Montgomery County and has no fiscal or direct operational impact on state education administration.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill modifies the disclosure procedures for child abuse and neglect records when a child suffers a fatality or near fatality while in the custody of a state or local department, in foster care, or the subject of an agency investigation, report, referral, or complaint. It requires the local director of social services or the Secretary of Human Services to disclose specified reports and records within 30 days of receiving a request, requires prompt notification to the State's Attorney's office, and allows the State's Attorney 30 days to redact information that would seriously hinder a criminal prosecution.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Human Services, local departments of social services, and local State's Attorney's offices
qa_results.stakeholders: Children who are victims of abuse or neglect resulting in fatality or near fatality, foster parents, local departments of social services, State's Attorneys, and individuals or entities requesting public child abuse and neglect case records.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 1209 directly amends the Human Services Article governing the mandatory disclosure of child abuse and neglect records in cases of child fatalities or near fatalities. The Secretary of Human Services and local directors of social services are directly responsible for administering disclosures within specified timeframes, coordinating with State's Attorneys, and creating the disclosure form.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Maryland Values Act requires federal law enforcement officers to notify designated local or State officials prior to taking immigration enforcement actions at sensitive locations, such as public schools, libraries, courthouses, and government healthcare facilities. It directs public schools, libraries, and State and local executive agencies at sensitive locations to bar federal immigration enforcement from nonpublic areas without a valid federal judicial warrant or exigent circumstances. Additionally, the Act mandates that the Attorney General publish guidance regarding immigration enforcement at sensitive locations, requires covered entities to adopt conforming policies by October 1, 2025, and directs governmental entities, in consultation with the Department of Information Technology, to establish procedures by July 1, 2026, to prevent the commercial sale and redisclosure of personal records and geolocation data.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General, Department of Information Technology, and State and local governmental entities
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland residents, immigrant communities, federal law enforcement officers, State and local law enforcement, and staff and visitors at public schools, libraries, courthouses, and State/local healthcare facilities
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Attorney General to develop and publish guidance regarding immigration enforcement at sensitive locations and grants the Attorney General the authority to designate additional locations that require special consideration.

The bill requires all governmental entities to consult with the Department of Information Technology to develop and publish procedures preventing the sale and redisclosure of personal records and geolocation data.

Facilities operated by the Comptroller are explicitly defined as sensitive locations, requiring the agency to implement policies restricting nonpublic access by federal immigration authorities and adopting policies consistent with Attorney General guidance.
Federal law enforcement officers conducting immigration enforcement actions at sensitive locations are required to provide notice to the Department of State Police barrack commander.

Public schools are designated as sensitive locations under the bill, requiring them to restrict nonpublic access to federal immigration enforcement officers without a federal court warrant and implement policies aligned with Attorney General guidance.

Public libraries are explicitly designated as sensitive locations, requiring public library systems overseen by the agency to deny access to nonpublic areas to immigration enforcement officers without a warrant and implement required policies.

State-operated health care facilities are defined as sensitive locations, requiring facilities managed by the Department of Health to restrict access to nonpublic areas and implement corresponding policies by October 1, 2025.

Federal law enforcement officers conducting immigration enforcement actions on property owned, leased, operated by, or under the control of the Department of Natural Resources must notify the Secretary of Natural Resources or the Secretary's designee.
Federal law enforcement officers conducting immigration enforcement on MDTA, MAA, or MPA property are required to notify the chief of police of the Maryland Transportation Authority.

The bill explicitly references property owned, leased, operated by, or under the control of the Maryland Aviation Administration regarding notification requirements for federal immigration enforcement actions.

The bill explicitly references property owned, leased, operated by, or under the control of the Maryland Port Administration regarding notification requirements for federal immigration enforcement actions.
Courthouses are categorized as sensitive locations under the bill, which impacts court facilities, operations, and policies regarding access by federal immigration enforcement.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the State Board of Cosmetologists to issue a limited license to provide eyelash extension services, alters the definition of esthetic services to include eyelash extensions, and establishes training, examination, apprenticeship, and curriculum standards for eyelash extension technicians.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Cosmetologists, Maryland Department of Labor
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals seeking to practice eyelash extension services, cosmetologists, beauty salon and barbershop owners, cosmetology schools, apprentices, and consumers receiving eyelash extension services.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures increase by approximately $25,000 in FY 2026 for one-time IT reprogramming of the board's licensing system. Special fund revenues to the State Barbers and Cosmetologists Boards' Fund increase beginning in FY 2026 from new biennial limited license fees (anticipated at $56 per license), though the exact total revenue is indeterminate. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Cosmetologists is housed within the Maryland Department of Labor. The department is directly responsible for implementing the new limited license for eyelash extension services, adopting regulations, updating licensing software, and collecting license fee revenues.

The bill requires the State Board of Cosmetologists to establish curriculum standards for use by the State Department of Education in approving cosmetology school applications and programs for instruction in eyelash extension services in public schools.
The bill requires curriculum standards to be used by the Maryland Higher Education Commission in approving applications and programs for eyelash extension instruction at private career schools.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters regulations concerning school bus stop locations in Montgomery County by delaying the requirement that prohibits bus stops on undivided highways with five or more lanes (unless a crossing guard or red-signal traffic control device is present) from December 31, 2026, to December 31, 2028. The bill also narrows the restriction to only apply to bus stops where at least 400 citations were issued in the preceding fiscal year to motorists traveling in the opposite direction.
qa_results.responsible_party: Montgomery County Public Schools and Montgomery County Government
qa_results.stakeholders: Montgomery County public school students, school bus drivers, motorists, and school crossing guards in Montgomery County.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are unaffected. Montgomery County expenditures may be reduced and delayed due to narrowing the scope of restricted school bus stop locations and extending the compliance deadline from December 31, 2026, to December 31, 2028. For context, the county estimated that hiring up to 13 crossing guards under current law requirements could cost more than $500,000 annually if bus stops could not be relocated. County revenues are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends § 7–801.1 of the Education Article concerning the placement and safety requirements of school bus stops on multi-lane highways in Montgomery County. The Maryland State Department of Education oversees the state's public education system and statewide standards for student transportation.

The legislation alters rules regarding school bus stops and traffic control devices on undivided highways with five or more lanes in Montgomery County, which encompasses state-maintained roadways and traffic signal systems under SHA's jurisdiction.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Maryland Department of Commerce, in coordination with specified county and university entities, to conduct a study on economic development and the tourist and visitor economy within the Montgomery County Agricultural Reserve, and to report its findings and policy recommendations to the Montgomery County Delegation by June 30, 2026.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Commerce
qa_results.stakeholders: Tourists, visitors, residents, and owners of small businesses, agricultural operations, historic sites, and recreation facilities within the Montgomery County Agricultural Reserve.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State and local expenditures are not significantly affected, as the Department of Commerce, the University of Maryland Extension, and Montgomery County can complete the study and report with existing budgeted resources. Revenues are not affected, and the impact on small businesses is minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Commerce is the lead agency designated to conduct the study on economic development and the tourist and visitor economy of the Montgomery County Agricultural Reserve, synthesize data, and submit the final report by June 30, 2026.
The bill explicitly mandates that the study be conducted in coordination with the University of Maryland Extension - Montgomery County, an entity within the University System of Maryland.

The Maryland Office of Tourism Development operates within the Division of Tourism, Film, and the Arts at the Department of Commerce and focuses on visitor economies and tourism attraction, which is the core subject of the required study.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill mandates that the Montgomery County Council and Prince George's County Council grant full or partial exemptions from the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission (WSSC) system development charge for specified properties and revitalization projects located in Montgomery County. It prohibits requiring applicants for Montgomery County exemptions to own the property, directs Montgomery County to approve exemptions on a first-come, first-served basis up to the annual limit including carryovers, and establishes annual reporting requirements for both Montgomery and Prince George's counties.
qa_results.responsible_party: Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission, Montgomery County Council, and Prince George's County Council
qa_results.stakeholders: Property developers, community-based youth organizations, child care providers, programs for developmentally disabled individuals, elderly housing facilities, biotechnology/manufacturing businesses in Montgomery County, and WSSC ratepayers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are unaffected. Local finances for the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission are not directly affected by expanding exemption eligibility, as both Montgomery and Prince George's counties operate under an existing $500,000 annual cap on exemptions with rollover provisions, and both counties currently retain substantial unused capacity under those limits.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Public Utilities Article concerning water and sewer system development charge exemptions administered by the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission and the local county councils. While the Public Service Commission was consulted as an information source for the fiscal note, it has no direct administrative or regulatory responsibilities under the bill and experiences no fiscal impact.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes municipalities in Queen Anne's County to lower the maximum speed limit on highways within their jurisdiction to as low as 15 miles per hour without conducting an engineering and traffic investigation.
qa_results.responsible_party: Municipal governments in Queen Anne's County
qa_results.stakeholders: Motorists, pedestrians, residents, and municipal governments in Queen Anne's County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues may increase minimally if lower speed limits result in additional speeding citations, with no significant operational impact on the District Court. Queen Anne's County municipal expenditures decrease minimally due to savings from not conducting engineering and traffic investigations before lowering speed limits.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Under Maryland transportation law, any alteration of speed limits by a local authority on a State highway or extension thereof requires approval by the State Highway Administration. The bill amends local speed-setting authority on highways within Queen Anne's County municipalities.

The bill amends the Transportation Article regarding speed limit regulations and traffic investigations, falling directly under MDOT's statutory domain and oversight of highway safety and regulations.
The fiscal note notes that general fund revenues and District Court caseload may be minimally affected by citations resulting from any lowered speed limits implemented under the bill.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill establishes a liquor tasting license in Somerset County, authorizing the Board of License Commissioners to issue the license to holders of a Class A beer, wine, and liquor license. It permits complimentary liquor tastings with per-person limits of one-half ounce per offering and up to five offerings per day, and establishes tiered license fees based on the number of tasting days.
qa_results.responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Somerset County
qa_results.stakeholders: Holders of Class A beer, wine, and liquor licenses in Somerset County, Somerset County retail consumers, and Somerset County local government.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Somerset County revenues will increase to the extent that liquor tasting licenses are issued, with tiered fees of $20 for 1 day, $200 for 26 days, $300 for 52 days, and $400 for 104 days per licensing period. Any additional local enforcement activity can be absorbed within existing county resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the state's alcohol industry. While this bill is implemented locally by the Somerset County Board of License Commissioners and has no state fiscal impact, it relates to the regulation and licensing of alcoholic beverages within the state.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits health insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and health maintenance organizations—including pharmacy benefits managers acting on their behalf—from excluding coverage for certain specialty drugs administered or dispensed by qualified in-network medical oncology providers, and sets criteria for reimbursement rates.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Health insurance carriers, pharmacy benefits managers (PBMs), in-network medical oncology providers dispensing specialty drugs, and patients receiving specialty oncology medications.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Minimal special fund revenue increase for the Maryland Insurance Administration in FY 2026 from the $125 rate and form filing fee. Any regulatory workload can be absorbed within existing budgeted resources. No impact on local finances or the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of private insurance plans, health maintenance organizations, and pharmacy benefits managers in Maryland, the Maryland Insurance Administration is responsible for enforcing the bill's coverage and reimbursement mandates and reviewing insurer form filings.

The bill explicitly references the Health Services Cost Review Commission to clarify that the new coverage and reimbursement restrictions do not supersede the Commission's statutory authority to set rates for specialty drugs administered in regulated hospital settings.

The Department of Health houses the Health Services Cost Review Commission and oversees regulations governing health care practitioners authorized to administer and dispense specialty drugs under the Health Occupations Article.

The Department of Budget and Management was analyzed during the legislative review to evaluate the bill's potential fiscal effect on the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program, though it was determined to have no impact.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill formally establishes and codifies the Maryland Developmental Disabilities Administration Waiver Advisory Council within the Developmental Disabilities Administration. The council is tasked with advising and providing recommendations regarding system design, service delivery, federal waiver assurances, and quality enhancement strategies for Medicaid waiver programs, while prioritizing input from individuals with lived experience.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Developmental Disabilities Administration within the Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities participating in Medicaid waiver programs, their families, service providers, and disability advocacy organizations.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures can likely be absorbed with existing budgeted resources (such as member expense reimbursements and travel arrangements), as the bill generally codifies the existing council. State revenues are not affected, and there is no material fiscal effect on local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill formally establishes the Waiver Advisory Council within the Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA), an administration of the Department of Health. The Secretary of Health appoints voting members and designates nonvoting members, DDA provides staff support, and MDH hosts the council's webpage.

The Secretary of Disabilities designates a representative to serve as a nonvoting member on the newly established advisory council, which aligns closely with the department's mission to coordinate and improve services for individuals with disabilities.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new permanent advisory council, the Maryland Developmental Disabilities Administration Waiver Advisory Council, to provide ongoing advice and recommendations on Medicaid waiver programs.

The State Superintendent of Schools is required to designate a representative from the Division of Rehabilitation Services within the Department of Education to serve as a nonvoting member of the council.
The Secretary of Housing and Community Development is required to designate a representative to serve as a nonvoting member of the advisory council.
The Secretary of Human Services is required to designate a representative to serve as a nonvoting member of the advisory council.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Doula and Birth Policy Transparency Act requires Maryland hospitals providing obstetric care to adopt and submit to the Maryland Department of Health policies concerning doula access, informed consent for significant medical interventions, and acceptance of patient transfers from home birth settings and licensed direct-entry midwives. It also directs the Department of Health to make these policies available to the public upon request and requires medical professional liability insurers to provide coverage information on obstetric services to the department upon request.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: Birthing parents and their families, doulas, direct-entry midwives and home birth practitioners, hospitals providing obstetric services, and medical professional liability insurers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $90,800 in FY 2026, which accounts for the bill's October 1, 2025 effective date and covers the hiring of one health facilities nurse surveyor within the Office of Health Care Quality to adopt regulations, track compliance, and investigate complaints. Annualized expenditures range from $108,400 in FY 2027 to $123,300 in FY 2030. State revenues and local finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary implementing agency for the bill. It is responsible for adopting regulations, receiving evidence of hospital policies regarding doulas, informed consent, and patient transfers, making these policies available to the public upon request, and requesting obstetric coverage information from medical professional liability insurers.

The bill amends the Insurance Article by enacting requirements related to medical professional liability insurers providing obstetric care coverage policies. As the state agency regulating the insurance industry and insurers operating in Maryland, the Maryland Insurance Administration oversees compliance and was consulted on the legislation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office handles medical malpractice claims and was consulted as an information source regarding the bill's provisions on informed consent for significant medical interventions and medical professional liability insurance.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Department of Social and Economic Mobility (DoSEM) as a principal department within the Executive Branch, headed by a Secretary appointed by the Governor. The bill consolidates and acts as the successor to three existing offices: the Governor's Office of Small, Minority, and Women Business Affairs, the Office of Social Equity in the Maryland Cannabis Administration, and the Office of Minority Business Enterprises in the Maryland Department of Transportation. It establishes the Department of Social and Economic Mobility Special Fund to fund the operations and administrative expenses of the Office of Social Equity and Office of Minority Business Enterprises, and directs coordination and reporting on statewide social equity programs.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Social and Economic Mobility
qa_results.stakeholders: Small, minority-, and women-owned business enterprises, individuals and communities disproportionately impacted by the enforcement of cannabis laws, state agency procurement staff, and transferred State personnel.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $2.3 million in FY 2026 ($2,298,254, of which $2.2 million is pre-budgeted) for 9 new administrative and legal staff, one-time moving costs ($1.0 million), rent, and operating expenses, with ongoing general fund costs ranging from $1.6 million to $1.8 million annually. Additionally, 57 existing positions and associated special and general funds are redirected from MDOT, MCA, and the Executive Department, with special fund revenues and expenditures flowing through the newly established DoSEM Special Fund ($5.4 million in FY 2026 and $4.2 million to $4.4 million annually thereafter). There is no direct local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill transfers the office and all of its staff, funding, and statutory responsibilities to become a constituent unit within the newly established Department of Social and Economic Mobility.

The bill transfers the Office of Social Equity out of the Maryland Cannabis Administration to the new department, while requiring ongoing coordination and consultation between MCA and the office on regulations and technical assistance.
The bill transfers the Office of Minority Business Enterprises out of MDOT into the new department and mandates that the Transportation Trust Fund continue to fund OMBE's operations.

DBM is tasked alongside the Governor with managing the transfer of personnel, positions, and funding to the new department, as well as overseeing budget and classification for newly created agency positions.

The bill establishes a new principal executive department, requires the Governor to appoint the Secretary and Executive Director of Social Equity, authorizes the transfer of budgeted positions and funds, and requires annual reports to the Governor.
The bill designates the Attorney General as the legal adviser to the new department and requires the assignment of Assistant Attorneys General and a designated principal counsel to the agency.

The Comptroller must account for the new Special Fund, administer the quarterly distribution of cannabis sales and use tax revenues to the fund, and consult with the Office of Social Equity regarding the Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund.
The State Treasurer is required to hold and invest the newly created Department of Social and Economic Mobility Special Fund.
The bill requires Commerce to collaborate with the Office of Social Equity in assisting businesses with obtaining financing under the Capital Access Program and the Cannabis Business Assistance Fund.
The bill requires annual MBE reporting to be submitted to the Board of Public Works.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners to issue a Class B beer and wine or beer, wine, and liquor on-sale license, as well as a dancing permit to a Class H license holder, for establishments located within 1,000 feet of a school situated at the Annapolis Mall.
qa_results.responsible_party: Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Restaurants, bars, and hospitality businesses near the Annapolis Mall, patrons seeking entertainment and alcoholic beverages, and the school located at the Annapolis Mall.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. The bill does not materially affect Anne Arundel County finances and operations, though minimal permit fee revenues ($200 to $400 annually per permit) may be collected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters local alcoholic beverages licensing and permit distance requirements in Anne Arundel County. While local licensing and enforcement are handled by the county's Board of License Commissioners and there is no state fiscal impact, the Comptroller is broadly responsible for regulating the state's alcohol industry.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill creates a limited special event permit in Anne Arundel County, allowing the Board of License Commissioners to issue single-day permits to certain alcoholic beverage license holders (Class B, C, D, and qualifying Class BLX and H licenses) to provide music, dancing, and other legal forms of entertainment.
qa_results.responsible_party: Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Anne Arundel County alcoholic beverages license holders (Class B, BLX, C, D, and H), patrons, and local performers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: The bill does not materially affect Anne Arundel County operations or finances, though it establishes permit fees of $15 per day for beer and wine licensees, $25 per day for beer, wine, and liquor licensees, and no fee for Class C licensees. Small business impact is minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article to authorize a limited special event permit in Anne Arundel County. While the permit is administered and issued locally by the Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners with no state fiscal impact, the Comptroller regulates the alcohol industry in the state.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes Charles County to regulate off-highway recreational vehicles (OHRVs), require county registration and associated fees, set age restrictions on their operation, and impound OHRVs involved in certain traffic violations or unauthorized use on public or private property.
qa_results.responsible_party: Charles County Government
qa_results.stakeholders: Owners and operators of off-highway recreational vehicles in Charles County, local law enforcement, and Charles County residents.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not directly affect State finances or operations. Because the bill is authorizing, it has no immediate local fiscal impact; however, if Charles County implements registration requirements and fees, county revenues will increase minimally, with no material impact on local expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Maryland Vehicle Law within the Transportation Article (§ 25-102) to grant Charles County specific regulatory, registration, and impoundment authority over off-highway recreational vehicles.

The Motor Vehicle Administration oversees statewide vehicle titling and registration. The bill establishes an exception allowing Charles County to implement county-level registration and fees for off-highway recreational vehicles.

Maryland State Police officers enforce the Maryland Vehicle Law and criminal laws throughout the state, including the reckless driving, impaired driving, and trespassing statutes referenced in the vehicle impoundment provisions.

The court system is responsible for adjudicating alleged violations of the Transportation Article and Criminal Law Article that could give rise to vehicle impoundment proceedings under local regulation.

qa_results.bill_summary: Renames 'network directory' to 'provider directory' to conform with federal law (the No Surprises Act) and shortens the timeframe within which health insurance carriers must update their online directory after receiving provider changes from 15 working days to 2 working days (retaining 15 working days for dental carriers). The bill also requires carriers to verify and update directory information at least once every 90 days, mandates specific disclaimer notices on printed directories, and requires the Insurance Commissioner to report to the General Assembly by January 1, 2026, regarding regulations related to provider directory accuracy.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Commissioner
qa_results.stakeholders: Health insurance carriers, dental plan carriers, healthcare providers, and health benefit plan enrollees and prospective enrollees in Maryland.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state or local fiscal impact. The bill pertains to private-sector requirements conforming to federal law. The Maryland Insurance Administration can complete the required report to the General Assembly using existing budgeted resources, and revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Insurance Article regarding provider directory requirements for health insurance carriers regulated by the state, and requires the Maryland Insurance Commissioner to enforce these standards and report to the General Assembly on regulatory changes related to directory accuracy by January 1, 2026.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Neighborhood Services Unit within the Baltimore City Sheriff's Office to partner with the Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners in enforcing local alcoholic beverages laws and executing other duties directed by the Sheriff. It also authorizes existing District Court civil case filing fee surcharge revenues to be used to fund the unit.
qa_results.responsible_party: Office of the Sheriff of Baltimore City and the Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Baltimore City residents, alcoholic beverage licensees in Baltimore City, and personnel within the Baltimore City Sheriff's Office and Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances and operations are not materially affected. Baltimore City faces a potential significant increase in expenditures, estimated at approximately $1,100,000 annually to hire 10 additional positions within the Sheriff's Office. City revenues are not materially affected, though existing court surcharge revenues may be redirected to support the new unit.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends § 7-301 of the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article regarding the authorized use of District Court filing fee surcharge revenues collected in Baltimore City, which are administered through the judicial branch supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill regulates earned wage access (EWA) products under the Maryland Consumer Loan Law and related consumer credit laws. It establishes licensing requirements for EWA providers through the Office of Financial Regulation, sets limits on fees for advances ($5 for advances up to $75, and $7.50 for advances over $75), requires providers to offer at least one no-cost option, prohibits charging interest or late fees, restricts debt collection and credit reporting practices, and establishes strict rules and disclosure mandates regarding tips or voluntary gratuities.
qa_results.responsible_party: Office of Financial Regulation (Maryland Department of Labor)
qa_results.stakeholders: Earned wage access providers, consumer lenders, employers, and consumers/employees who use earned wage access or consumer credit products.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill generally codifies existing practice and is not anticipated to materially affect State finances or operations. The Office of Financial Regulation can implement and enforce the provisions using existing resources. There is no local government fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill regulates earned wage access products under the Maryland Consumer Loan Law, overseen by the Commissioner of Financial Regulation, which is a division within the Maryland Department of Labor. The Department is responsible for licensing providers, receiving required annual reports, adopting implementing regulations, and conducting enforcement.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Labor and the Commissioner of Financial Regulation, and enforces state consumer protection laws regarding consumer credit practices.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Managed Aquifer Recharge Pilot Program within the Maryland Department of the Environment, prohibiting unauthorized groundwater augmentation while authorizing the department to review, permit, and regulate a single demonstration facility using treated reclaimed water to test groundwater augmentation.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment
qa_results.stakeholders: Local governments, public water systems, private well owners near potential project sites, and water treatment or engineering businesses.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: MDE can implement the program and issue the single permit using existing resources. General fund expenditures and revenues for MDH Laboratories Administration may increase by approximately $17,000 annually beginning as early as FY 2026 for water testing reimbursed by MDE. Local government expenditures may increase significantly if a local entity voluntarily applies for the permit and constructs a demonstration facility.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Managed Aquifer Recharge Pilot Program within MDE. MDE is the primary regulatory body responsible for accepting applications, issuing the managed aquifer recharge permit, setting water quality and monitoring requirements, conducting inspections, adopting regulations, and submitting annual reports.

MDH's Laboratories Administration provides analytical testing support for MDE and is anticipated to conduct water testing for the pilot program under an existing memorandum of understanding, resulting in an estimated $17,000 annual impact on expenditures and reimbursable revenues.

MDE is required to submit an annual report to the Governor beginning December 31, 2028, on the status and scientific results of the pilot program and recommendations regarding permanent statutory or regulatory authorization.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), the Maryland Children's Health Program, managed care organizations, and certain commercial health insurance carriers from requiring prior authorization for a patient transfer to a special pediatric hospital.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and Maryland Insurance Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Pediatric patients under age 22 (or under age 23 with co-occurring physical and behavioral health conditions) needing nonacute medical, rehabilitation, therapy, or palliative services; special pediatric hospitals; health insurance carriers; and Medicaid managed care organizations.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration increase minimally in FY 2026 from $125 rate and form filing fees. Medicaid expenditures (general and federal funds) may increase by an indeterminate but likely minimal amount beginning in FY 2026 to the extent the bill increases nonmedically necessary inpatient days, with federal fund revenues increasing accordingly. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health administers the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) and the Maryland Children's Health Program (MCHP), both of which are directly prohibited under the bill from requiring prior authorization for transfers to special pediatric hospitals.

The Maryland Insurance Administration regulates health insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and HMOs subject to the new prior authorization prohibition, and will review policy form filings and collect associated filing fees.

The Department of Budget and Management administers the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program; while reviewed as an information source, the fiscal note determined the bill has no fiscal impact on the State plan.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill revises Maryland's Prescription Drug Repository Program by allowing entities located in other states to participate as drop-off sites and repositories, and expanding the program to include over-the-counter (OTC) drugs in addition to prescription drugs. It establishes eligibility for patients through self-attestation as indigent, uninsured, underinsured, or enrolled in a public health benefits program; adjusts packaging and expiration date standards; permits certain transfers of donated inventory; and expands civil and criminal immunity protections for program participants and volunteers.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Pharmacy
qa_results.stakeholders: Eligible patients (individuals who are indigent, uninsured, underinsured, or enrolled in public health benefit programs), participating in-state and out-of-state pharmacies and repositories, pharmacy staff and volunteers, and drug donors.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State Board of Pharmacy special fund expenditures increase by $53,844 in FY 2026 to hire one full-time licensing specialist to handle registration and oversight of out-of-state participating entities, increasing to $69,800 by FY 2030 due to ongoing operational costs. State revenues are unaffected, and there is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Board of Pharmacy, which regulates and administers the Prescription Drug Repository Program, is housed within the Maryland Department of Health. The bill expands the program to include out-of-state entities and over-the-counter drugs, requiring MDH/the Board of Pharmacy to adopt regulations, register out-of-state participants, and incur special fund expenditures for staffing.
The State Board of Pharmacy is statutorily required to submit an annual report to the Governor on the operation of the Prescription Drug Repository Program.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes that CDC Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommendations governing vaccinations administered by pharmacists and child wellness insurance coverage refer to guidance in effect on December 31, 2024, or later for newly recommended vaccines. It also requires insurers and nonprofit health service plans to cover childhood and adolescent immunizations recommended by ACIP or the American Academy of Pediatrics as of December 31, 2024, without a deductible.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Administration and Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: Licensed pharmacists, commercial health insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and children and families receiving immunizations
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Minimal increase in special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration in FY 2026 only from the $125 rate and form filing fee. Form reviews can be managed using existing budgeted resources. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Insurance Article regarding mandated child wellness and immunization coverage, granting the Insurance Commissioner regulatory authority and resulting in rate and form filings submitted to the Administration.

The bill directly governs the scope of pharmacist-administered vaccinations, establishes criteria for vaccination protocols in consultation with health occupations licensing boards, and references reporting requirements to the Department's ImmuNet system.
As the agency overseeing the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program, DBM assesses health insurance coverage mandates for potential fiscal and benefit design impacts.

qa_results.bill_summary: Known as Matthew's Law, this bill prohibits operating a gasoline-powered vessel manufactured after July 31, 2007, that has accommodation spaces, swim platforms, or aft lounging areas on Maryland waters unless carbon monoxide warning labels are conspicuously affixed near the transom and helm. It also specifies that the Department of Natural Resources may not impose a penalty for violations.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources
qa_results.stakeholders: Owners and operators of qualifying gasoline-powered vessels, boat passengers, and maritime recreationists in Maryland waters
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local government finances, and has a minimal effect on small businesses. The Department of Natural Resources is prohibited from imposing penalties for violations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill adds a safety requirement to the State Boat Act in the Natural Resources Article requiring carbon monoxide warning labels on certain gasoline-powered vessels on State waters, and explicitly prohibits the Department of Natural Resources from imposing penalties for violations.

qa_results.bill_summary: Exempts Garrett County from the requirement to advertise for competitive bids in local newspapers for contracts involving an indeterminate amount of goods or services procured on an as-needed basis over time (regardless of total value) and vehicle purchases up to $100,000.
qa_results.responsible_party: Garrett County Commissioners and Garrett County government
qa_results.stakeholders: Garrett County government, Garrett County taxpayers, and vendors or contractors bidding on county contracts or selling vehicles to the county
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: May result in minimal cost savings for Garrett County from reduced advertising expenses and improved operational efficiencies.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes a special event venue beer, wine, and liquor license in Caroline County, allowing qualified venue owners to sell alcoholic beverages for on-premises consumption at a tiered annual fee based on the number of events. It also permits multiple event license holders to store alcoholic beverages securely on premises between events, subject to specific inventory and recordkeeping requirements.
qa_results.responsible_party: Caroline County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Owners and operators of special event venues and holders of multiple event licenses (including volunteer fire companies) in Caroline County, alcohol wholesalers, and event attendees.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: Caroline County revenues will increase beginning in FY 2026 depending on the number of licenses issued, with fees set at $250 (up to 10 events), $500 (up to 20 events), $750 (up to 30 events), and $1,000 (up to 40 events) per year. County enforcement can be handled with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes personnel of the Comptroller of Maryland to inspect the alcoholic beverage inventory records and premises of multiple event license holders in Caroline County.

qa_results.bill_summary: Exempts personal property used in connection with certain registered large family child care homes from taxation and valuation in Anne Arundel County. It also authorizes Anne Arundel County and its municipalities to grant a real property tax credit of up to $10,000 for qualifying portions of real property dedicated exclusively to licensed or registered child care centers, large family child care homes, or adult and elderly day care centers.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
qa_results.stakeholders: Operators of large family child care homes, child care centers, and adult/elderly day care facilities in Anne Arundel County; businesses with 25 or more employees offering child care facilities; and Anne Arundel County and municipal governments.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Local property tax revenues in Anne Arundel County and its municipalities will decrease beginning in FY 2026 due to the personal property tax exemption (expected to be minimal as only one such home was licensed as of January 2025) and local property tax credits of up to $10,000 per qualifying property to the extent local governments authorize and grant them. Local expenditures are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill bases eligibility for local property tax exemptions and credits on child care facilities and family child care homes registered or licensed by MSDE under Title 9.5 of the Education Article.
The bill references day care centers for the elderly and adults licensed under Title 14 of the Health - General Article, which falls under MDH regulatory oversight.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Department of General Services to conduct an assessment of State-owned facilities operated by the 16 State agencies it supports to determine their suitability and availability for leasing to child care centers, and to report and publish its findings by December 1, 2026.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of General Services
qa_results.stakeholders: Child care providers, Maryland working families and children, and State agencies occupying State-owned facilities.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $96,000 in FY 2026 and $35,500 in FY 2027 to hire one contractual program manager to review facilities, conduct site visits, and prepare the required report. No impact on revenues or local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DGS is the primary implementing agency tasked with conducting the assessment of all State-owned facilities across 16 supported agencies to determine their suitability and availability for leasing to child care centers, and reporting its findings to the General Assembly.

MSDE oversees early childhood development and child care center licensing standards (under § 9.5–401 of the Education Article), requiring extensive collaboration with DGS to assess whether facility physical plants meet child care center regulatory criteria.

qa_results.bill_summary: Exempts certified security guards employed by or providing services to cannabis licensees or registrants from having to complete a separate criminal history records check to register as cannabis agents with the Maryland Cannabis Administration. Additionally, alters the definition of "security guard employer" to exclude video lottery operators, sports wagering facility licensees, and health care facilities from security guard employer regulations.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of State Police and the Maryland Cannabis Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Security guards, cannabis licensees and registrants, video lottery operators, sports wagering facility licensees, and health care facilities
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $75,000 in FY 2026 for one-time IT costs for the Department of State Police to update its online licensing portal. General fund revenues decrease indeterminately beginning in FY 2026 from reduced security guard certification and renewal fees. Special fund revenues and expenditures for the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services decrease indeterminately beginning in FY 2026 due to fewer criminal history records checks and associated pass-through FBI fees. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of State Police is responsible for licensing security guard agencies and certifying security guards under Title 19 of the Business Occupations and Professions Article. The bill directly impacts MSP's regulatory scope by altering the definition of 'security guard employer,' requiring $75,000 in IT expenditures to update its application portal and resulting in reduced certification fee revenues.

The bill directly amends § 36-501 of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article by exempting certain cannabis agents who are already authorized security guards from the requirement to obtain a separate State and national criminal history records check to register with the MCA.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department houses the Criminal Justice Information System Central Repository (CJIS-CR), which processes criminal history records checks. The bill will reduce the volume of CHRCs processed, resulting in minor decreases in special fund fee revenues and FBI pass-through expenditures.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly references video lottery operators and sports wagering facility licensees licensed and regulated by the agency, exempting them from the definition and regulatory requirements of 'security guard employers.'

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill shortens the timeframe within which health insurance carriers must accept or reject certain behavioral health care professionals—including licensed master social workers, certain graduate-level counselors and therapists, registered psychology associates, licensed certified social workers-clinical, and licensed clinical professional counselors—for participation on a provider panel to within 60 days after receiving a completed application. It also updates the statutory list of community-based behavioral health providers whom carriers may not reject solely based on practicing within their scope of license by removing licensed graduate social workers to reflect current licensing titles.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Health insurance carriers, behavioral health care professionals (such as licensed master social workers, graduate counselors and therapists, psychology associates, and clinical counselors), accredited community-based behavioral health programs, and patients seeking behavioral health services.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not substantively change State activities or operations, and local government finances and operations are not directly affected. Small business community-based health care providers may experience a meaningful impact by being able to credential providers faster and obtain insurance reimbursement more quickly.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Insurance Article regarding health insurance carriers' credentialing timelines and requirements for behavioral health care provider panels, which are regulated and enforced by the Maryland Insurance Administration through existing statutory penalties.

The bill affects provider panel credentialing for behavioral health professionals licensed by health occupations boards housed within MDH (such as social workers, professional counselors, and psychology associates) and references community-based health service programs accredited under MDH regulations.

qa_results.bill_summary: Expands health insurance coverage requirements for medically appropriate and necessary adult hearing aids to include those that are ordered, fitted, and dispensed by a licensed hearing aid dispenser, in addition to licensed audiologists.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Adult health insurance policyholders needing hearing aids, licensed hearing aid dispensers, and health insurance carriers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Minimal increase in special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration from $125 rate and form filing fees in FY 2026 only, with additional workload managed using existing budgeted resources. There is no impact on the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program and no material effect on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary regulatory agency responsible for enforcing health insurance mandates and reviewing rate and form filings submitted by insurers to comply with the altered hearing aid coverage requirements.
The Department of Budget and Management oversees the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program, which must evaluate changes to state health insurance coverage mandates.

The Maryland Health Benefit Exchange oversees qualified health plans and essential health benefits offered on the individual and small business marketplaces, which are subject to state coverage mandates.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing coordinates policies and advocates for improved accessibility and resources, including hearing health coverage and devices, for hard of hearing residents across Maryland.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes a civil penalty of up to $50,000 per day for any person who falsifies information submitted in a lead-contaminated dust testing or visual inspection report required under the Reduction of Lead Risk in Housing law.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment
qa_results.stakeholders: Accredited lead paint inspectors and risk assessors, rental property owners, and tenants residing in affected rental housing.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues to the Lead Poisoning Prevention Fund may minimally increase beginning in FY 2026 from civil penalties assessed under the bill. State expenditures and local government finances and operations are not anticipated to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) administers the Lead Poisoning Prevention Program and receives the verified inspection and testing reports under Title 6, Subtitle 8 of the Environment Article. The bill establishes a civil penalty of up to $50,000 for falsifying information in these reports, which will be collected and deposited into the Lead Poisoning Prevention Fund.

The bill provides that the civil penalty is to be collected via a civil action, which directly involves the Maryland state court system managed and supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

As the chief legal representative for state agencies, the Office of the Attorney General would represent the Department of the Environment in filing and litigating civil actions to collect civil penalties for falsified lead inspection reports.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration to enter into agreements through a national association of motor vehicle agencies to facilitate the issuance, use, and verification of electronic credentials, and allows individuals to present a valid electronic credential (mobile ID) instead of a physical driver's license when renting a vehicle.
qa_results.responsible_party: Motor Vehicle Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Drivers utilizing electronic credentials or mobile IDs, nonresidents renting vehicles in Maryland, and vehicle rental companies and lessors.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no material impact on Transportation Trust Fund revenues or expenditures. To the extent the Motor Vehicle Administration enters into facilitation agreements, it can do so using existing resources. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends laws governing the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), authorizing it to enter into agreements through a national association of motor vehicle agencies to facilitate electronic credentials and permitting electronic credentials to be used in rental vehicle transactions.

The Department of Transportation is the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration, and the bill impacts Transportation Article provisions and operates within MDOT's administrative and budgetary oversight.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes tow trucks to be equipped with and display mounted portable variable messaging signs while at the scene of a vehicle crash or disabled vehicle, provided the signs conform to standards in the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices and display only messages approved by the State Highway Administration.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Highway Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Tow truck operators, motorists, highway maintenance personnel, and emergency responders.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is authorizing in nature and does not directly affect State or local revenues or expenditures. However, expenditures may increase if State or local agencies voluntarily choose to equip or purchase tow trucks with portable variable messaging signs (for illustrative purposes, the Maryland Transportation Authority estimated fleet purchase costs of $3.0 million for 20 trucks at $150,000 each).

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the State Highway Administration (SHA) with adopting the standards in the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices that portable variable messaging signs must conform to, as well as approving the specific messages authorized for display.

The bill amends the Transportation Article regarding vehicle equipment regulations and directly affects its modal administrations, including the State Highway Administration and the Maryland Transportation Authority.

MDTA operates highway facilities and tow truck fleets; the fiscal note specifically highlights potential fiscal impacts if MDTA chooses to purchase and deploy tow trucks equipped with portable variable messaging signs.
The Maryland State Police was an information source for the fiscal note and is responsible for enforcing vehicle lighting and equipment laws on Maryland highways.
The bill amends vehicle equipment and lighting provisions under the Maryland Vehicle Law, which is administered and regulated by the Motor Vehicle Administration.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill reduces the liability limits and damages caps for previously time-barred civil actions for child sexual abuse filed on or after June 1, 2025. Specifically, it lowers the noneconomic damages cap from $1.5 million to $700,000 for non-governmental defendants, and reduces the liability limits under the Maryland Tort Claims Act, Local Government Tort Claims Act, and for county boards of education from $890,000 to $400,000 for a single claimant. It also limits attorney's fees to 20% of a settlement or 25% of a judgment, bars actions against the State or State units filed on or after January 1, 2026 for previously time-barred claims, and establishes reporting requirements for the Judiciary.
qa_results.responsible_party: Supreme Court of Maryland and Maryland Judiciary
qa_results.stakeholders: Claimants of child sexual abuse, plaintiffs' attorneys, the State of Maryland, local governments, and county boards of education.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State and local expenditures decrease, potentially significantly, due to lower liability caps ($400,000) for previously time-barred claims filed on or after June 1, 2025, and applying limits per claimant rather than per occurrence. State and local revenues are unaffected. Exact fiscal savings cannot be reliably determined in advance.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Section 3 of the bill directly mandates that the Maryland Judiciary report annually to the General Assembly beginning January 31, 2027, on the amount of each award made under the Act and a summary of the underlying sexual abuse claims. Additionally, Section 2 authorizes the Supreme Court of Maryland to adopt implementation rules.

The OAG represents the State in civil litigation and tort claims under the Maryland Tort Claims Act (MTCA). The bill directly impacts the defense and potential liability for thousands of pending and future Child Victims Act claims filed against the State by setting liability caps and establishing a filing deadline of January 1, 2026, for claims against the State.

The Treasurer's Office administers the State Insurance Trust Fund (SITF), which handles and pays tort claims against the State under the Maryland Tort Claims Act. The bill directly alters MTCA liability caps for child sexual abuse claims, significantly impacting potential state liabilities and SITF expenditures.

The bill amends Section 4-105 of the Education Article, requiring the State Board of Education to update its standards for comprehensive liability insurance coverage carried by county boards of education to conform to the new liability caps for sexual abuse claims.

Under the amended provisions of Education Article § 4-105, county boards of education that elect to self-insure must comply with regulations adopted by the State Insurance Commissioner and submit their self-insurance terms and conditions to the Commissioner for review and approval.
As the State's principal fiscal agency, DBM is affected by potential substantial reductions in State expenditures and liabilities arising from the modified MTCA caps and settlement considerations.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Maryland Department of Health, in coordination with the Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems, to adopt regulations by October 1, 2026, establishing minimum perinatal care standards that meet or exceed the Maryland Perinatal System Standards. Hospitals providing obstetrical services and freestanding birthing centers must comply with these standards as a condition of licensure.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: Hospitals providing obstetrical services, freestanding birthing centers, healthcare professionals, and patients receiving perinatal and neonatal care
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems can develop regulations and enforce compliance using existing budgeted resources. There is no effect on state revenues and no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly requires the Maryland Department of Health, through regulations, to establish minimum perinatal care standards meeting or exceeding the Maryland Perinatal System Standards and enforce them as a condition of licensure for hospitals offering obstetrical services and freestanding birthing centers.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates that the Maryland Department of Health coordinate with the Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems (MIEMSS) to adopt regulations establishing the minimum perinatal care standards.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the holder of a Class D alcoholic beverages license, or an employee of the license holder, to deliver alcoholic beverages within Howard County subject to certain requirements and verification procedures.
qa_results.responsible_party: Howard County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Class D alcoholic beverages license holders, their employees, and adult consumers purchasing alcohol for delivery in Howard County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: There is no state fiscal effect, and Howard County finances and operations are not materially affected. Small businesses holding a Class D license in Howard County are expected to see increased sales and revenue from offering delivery services.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is responsible for collecting alcoholic beverage excise and sales taxes and possesses broad statutory duties related to the regulation and taxation of the alcohol industry in Maryland. While this bill strictly affects local Class D retail licensees delivering within Howard County and has no direct state fiscal impact, it pertains directly to alcoholic beverages laws.

qa_results.bill_summary: House Bill 1424, titled the Protect Our Federal Workers Act, expands the purposes of the Catastrophic Event Account and renames and expands the Federal Government Shutdown Employee Assistance Loan Fund to provide no-interest loans and financial assistance to Maryland residents who are federal employees facing furloughs, mass layoffs, closures, or relocations. It authorizes loan forgiveness, increases the annual mandated appropriation to the Office of the Attorney General from $1.0 million to at least $2.5 million to protect Marylanders against certain federal actions, and creates a temporary Expedited Hiring Program in the Department of Budget and Management to quickly recruit former federal employees into vacant State positions.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor, Department of Budget and Management, and Office of the Attorney General
qa_results.stakeholders: Current and former federal employees and contractors residing in Maryland who are impacted by federal shutdowns, mass layoffs, or facility closures, as well as State and county agencies seeking to fill vacant government positions.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State Rainy Day Fund expenditures increase by $6.5 million in FY 2025 to transfer $5.0 million to the loan fund and $1.5 million to the Office of the Attorney General (OAG). Dedicated Purpose Account expenditures increase by $500,000 in FY 2025 and $1.5 million in FY 2026 to support the Expedited Hiring Program. Catastrophic Event Account expenditures increase by $10.0 million in FY 2026 for loan capitalization, resulting in special fund loan expenditures of up to $15.0 million in FY 2026. General fund expenditures increase by $1.7 million in FY 2026 for Department of Labor administrative and IT costs, and by $1.5 million annually beginning in FY 2027 to satisfy the increased mandated appropriation for OAG. Local fiscal impact is minimal, though counties may benefit from expedited hiring coordination.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Administers the newly renamed and expanded Federal Government Employee Assistance Loan Fund, establishes loan procedures and eligibility, processes loans and loan forgiveness, and conducts research and reports on foreclosure activity among federal workers.

Establishes and administers the temporary Expedited Hiring Program to recruit former federal workers into the State Personnel Management System, develops guidance and regulations, and oversees the Catastrophic Event Account.

Receives expanded authority under the Maryland Defense Act to investigate and litigate federal actions impacting federal employees and federal benefits/entitlements, and receives an increased annual mandated appropriation of at least $2.5 million to employ attorneys.

Authorizes the Governor to execute transfers from the Revenue Stabilization Account and Catastrophic Event Account, mandates funding in the Governor's annual budget for the Attorney General, and establishes notice and review procedures between the Attorney General and the Governor before litigation is filed.

Accounts for the Catastrophic Event Account and the Federal Government Employee Assistance Loan Fund, and is authorized to disclose tax information to the Department of Labor to verify eligibility and prevent fraud.
Holds and manages investments for the Catastrophic Event Account and the Federal Government Employee Assistance Loan Fund as specified in the State Finance and Procurement statutory alterations.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires circuit courthouses constructed or undergoing major renovations on or after October 1, 2025, to provide a private lactation room equipped with specific amenities for employees and the public. The bill also authorizes jury officials to excuse breastfeeding mothers and primary caregivers of children under the age of three from jury service, and requires the Maryland Judiciary to collect and report annual data on jury duty excusals.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary
qa_results.stakeholders: Breastfeeding mothers, court visitors, court employees, primary caregivers of children under three years of age, prospective jurors, and county circuit courts.
